title: Visible-light degradation of ciprofloxacin by hierarchical Ag 3 PO 4 /CuInS 2  heterostructures: interfacial charge transfer, transformation pathways, and ecological risk context
content: Ciprofloxacin persists in aquatic environments and may contribute to antimicrobial resistance, creating demand for efficient, low-energy treatment technologies. In this study, a hierarchical flower-like Ag3PO4/CuInS2 heterostructure was synthesized through a combined solvothermal–hydrothermal route and evaluated for visible-light-driven ciprofloxacin degradation. XRD, FTIR, Raman, XPS and elemental mapping confirmed the coexistence and interfacial coupling of cubic Ag3PO4 and chalcopyrite CuInS2. The heterostructure consisted of faceted Ag3PO4 particles integrated with flower-like CuInS2 aggregates and exhibited a surface area of 39.22 m2 g−1, average pore diameter of 47.70 nm and band gap of 1.92 eV. Photoluminescence quenching and a reduced impedance arc indicated improved interfacial charge migration and suppressed electron–hole recombination. Under visible light, the composite achieved 96.13% ciprofloxacin degradation within 60 min, compared with 44.30% for Ag3PO4 and 58.87% for CuInS2, with a rate constant of 0.03561 min−1, 5.3 and 3.76 times higher, respectively. Maximum degradation occurred near pH 6.6, while excessive catalyst loading and higher ciprofloxacin concentration reduced efficiency. Radical-quenching experiments showed that photogenerated holes and hydroxyl radicals were the dominant oxidative species, with superoxide making a secondary contribution. A direct Z-scheme-like pathway was proposed, retaining strongly oxidizing holes in the Ag3PO4 valence band and reducing electrons in the CuInS2 conduction band. LC-MS indicated piperazine oxidation, N-dealkylation, ring opening, defluorination, decarboxylation and quinolone-ring cleavage. The heterostructure retained 89.45% degradation efficiency after four cycles, indicating promising reusability. These findings demonstrate enhanced charge separation, rapid antibiotic transformation, improved photocatalytic performance and promising visible-light treatment potential of antibiotic-contaminated water.
